content: The United States Congress passed a legislative act in honor of Ryan White, a teenager from Indiana who contracted AIDS in 1984 through a contaminated hemophilia treatment. Following his diagnosis, he was expelled from school due to the stigma surrounding the disease. Ryan White became a prominent advocate for AIDS research and public awareness until his death on April 8, 1990. This act represents the largest federally funded program in the United States dedicated to supporting individuals living with HIV/AIDS. Its primary goal was to secure funding to enhance access to medical care for low-income, uninsured, and underinsured individuals affected by AIDS, as well as their families. Unlike Medicare or Medicaid, the Ryan White programs operate as a payer of last resort, meaning they provide financial support for treatment only when no other resources are available. As the AIDS epidemic expanded, funding for the program increased significantly. In 1991, the first year funds were allocated, approximately $220 million was spent. By the early 2000s, this amount had grown nearly tenfold. The Ryan White Care Act was reauthorized in 1996, 2000, and 2006. The program provides some level of care to approximately 500,000 individuals annually and, in 2004, distributed funds to 2,567 organizations. These programs also support local and state primary medical care providers, offer support services, train healthcare providers, and provide technical assistance to organizations involved in HIV/AIDS care. As of 2005, about one-third of the program's funding was allocated to the AIDS Drug Assistance Program (ADAP), which primarily focuses on providing FDA-approved prescription medications to those in need. The Ryan White Care Act was scheduled for reauthorization at the end of 2005. However, Congress was unable to reach an agreement on proposed changes, and the act was extended for one year under its existing terms. Prior to the 2006 reauthorization, funding allocations were based on the proportion of patients with advanced AIDS in each region. The 2006 reauthorization introduced a revised allocation mechanism that also considered the number of individuals living with HIV infection, not just those with full-blown AIDS. A significant portion of the act's funding is designated as emergency relief for Eligible Metropolitan Areas (EMAs). The 2006 reauthorization redefined EMAs as cities with populations exceeding 50,000, a change from the previous threshold of 500,000.
